baseBlurb: Sam comes back from two nights away and the flat has to say hello properly, without overdoing it.

stories.blurb: Dad is home from a trade fair, Mum is stirring pots, and one flat word in the hall tells you a lot.

opener.setting: Thursday, 6:10pm. Mum and Dad's hallway. Dad is back from two nights at a trade fair in another city.

lines.text: “Your dad needs a proper welcome, or he eats in silence and addresses his remarks to the potatoes.”
lines.cue: from the kitchen, not turning round
in the doorway, coat zipped, a carrier bag of fridge magnets in one hand

opener.ask: How much of a welcome does Dad need after being away, and how do you build one that pays it?

rounds.label: Spot, round 1
rounds.intro: Three lines from the hello in the hall. Tap what each one tells you.

items.cue: after your quick “Hi” as his suitcase rolls past you down the hall
options: He's glad to be home
He's counting, and your hello was short
He wants to tell you about the fair
items.why: He is counting. A short hello leaves him owed, and a flat “fine” is how owed sounds in his house.

traps.0: Glad would come with a bigger word, or a look at the family. “Fine” aimed at the hall wall is flat, so calling it gladness misreads it.
traps.2: Wanting to tell you about the fair would come with a hook, like “You won't believe the hotel.” He is wheeling away, so no hook is on offer.

items.example:
A bus driver, early shift.
You say “Morning” while looking at your phone.
“Yep,” he says. He wanted a little more than that.

items.cue: laughing, after four warm lines in a row at the door
options: A pile of warm lines sounds like cover
He's tired from the trip and wants some quiet
He's teasing because the welcome was just right
items.why: Too many warm lines at once sound like cover for bad news. He is checking what the pile is hiding.

traps.1: Tired would show as short answers and a slump, not a joke. He is laughing, so the question is about the warmth.
traps.2: A welcome that was just right would get a smile and a story. A joke about breakages means the pile of lines made him suspicious.

items.example:
A neighbour's retirement card.
“Brilliant, wonderful, we'll all miss you, such a star!”
“Who's been at the cake?” he says. Too much shine looks like cover.

items.text: “Right, I'd better find Leo's PE bag.”
items.cue: the hallway, straight after a quick hello
options: A compliment
A question about the trip
A quick exit
items.why: A quick exit. It ends the greeting, and it counts as one small nod about your evening, not a welcome for him.

traps.0: A compliment would say something nice about him. This line is about a PE bag, so it can't be one.
traps.1: A question about the trip would ask him for something. The line asks for nothing and closes the talk instead.

items.example:
A school corridor.
“Sorry, got to dash, the bell's gone!”
It is polite. It is still a single nod, and the talk is over.

rounds.label: Play, the week in motion
rounds.intro: Dad's greeting is a counter. Pick the lines that pay what he is owed, then meet Mrs Kale on the stairs.

items.prompt: Dad is back from the trade fair after two nights away and is owed about a dozen nods. Build a greeting that pays them.

palette.text: “Wait, tell me everything about the hotel.”
“I missed you. The house was far too quiet without you.”
“Right, I'd better find Leo's PE bag.”

items.underMsg: Dad says “Fine.” and the suitcase wheels carry him upstairs. He is still owed more than that.
items.overMsg: Dad laughs. “All right, what have you broken?” A pile of warm lines looks like cover for bad news.
items.hitMsg: He sits on the bottom stair, unlaces one shoe, and starts on the hotel breakfast.
items.why: What is owed grows with time apart. Two nights asks for a good deal more than a hello in passing and a good deal less than a month would. Too little leaves a person flat, and too much sounds like cover.

items.title: Thursday, 6:25 and 6:40pm, the stairs
items.setting: Mrs Kale on the landing with a parcel, first as you go down for the takeaway and then as you come back up with it.

beats.cue: stairs, 6:25, a parcel under one arm

lines.outcome: She answers at once, pleased to be asked for nothing.
lines.why: A hello with her name in it is a clean exchange. It pays a nod each way.

lines.outcome: She tells the parcel it's a chilly one.
lines.why: A nod with no word is smaller. It leaves her to carry the exchange alone.

beats.text: “Evening, dear. Is your father home? This came for him, and it rattles.”
beats.cue: still on the landing, the parcel held out in both hands

lines.text: “He is, thank you. I'll take it up to him.”
lines.outcome: She hands it over and listens to it rattle once more. “Fragile. Mind.”
lines.why: You answered what she asked, not only the hello. That keeps the exchange going.

lines.outcome: “Yes, yes,” she says to your back, the parcel still in the air.
lines.why: The words fit, but you left before she finished. It ends the exchange a half-step early.

beats.cue: stairs, 6:40, second pass with the takeaway. She is straightening the doormat.

lines.text: A nod and a half-smile, then keep moving.
lines.outcome: She nods back and goes on with the mat.
lines.why: A small nod is enough for a quick second pass. You asked for nothing, so nothing more is owed.

lines.text: “Mrs Kale! How's the hip? Did the plumber come? Is your sister still staying?”
lines.outcome: “Same as fifteen minutes ago,” she says. “What do you want?”
lines.why: Three questions on a second pass read as a favour about to be asked. The interest was real, and the pile of it felt like a pitch.

lines.outcome: Mrs Kale, to the doormat: “Hm.”
lines.why: Going by without a look is cold, and she notices. It is a small cut that leaves her owed.

items.example:
A caretaker in an office block.
“Morning, love, you look cold.” Every day, the same line, and a day without it gets noticed.

items.text: “Hi, Dad.” felt too small, and “Tell me everything about the hotel” felt like too much. What explains that?
options: Welcomes are only good manners, so any polite line will do and the number never matters
Time apart sets how much is owed, so too little and too much both land wrong
Dad is just hard to please, so whatever you say he will find a fault in it
items.why: A greeting is a precise exchange. Time apart sets how much is owed. Too little leaves a gap, and too much reads as cover.

traps.0: If it were only manners, the amount would not matter. Dad's “Fine” came after a short hello because a short hello carries a debt.
traps.2: “He's hard to please” is a shrug, and then you stop trying. The debt stays unpaid and the flat “fine” comes back tomorrow.

items.example:
A niece visiting after two years.
“Hi!” at the door, and then nothing for an hour.
The niece notices the gap in the welcome, even if nobody says so.

stories.blurb: Ruby is back from a wedding with a bag of cake, and her friends have one chance at the hello.

opener.setting: Saturday, 10:15am. The Corner Table, the window seat. Ruby has been at her cousin's wedding for two nights and is about to come through the door.

lines.text: “Ruby counts these things. Last time nobody said a word for ten minutes and she's still bringing it up.”
lines.cue: stirring a third sugar into his tea
at the door, hat in one hand, a paper bag of wedding cake in the other

opener.ask: How much of a welcome does Ruby need after being away, and how do you build one that pays it?

rounds.label: Spot, round 1
rounds.intro: Three lines from the hello at the door. Tap what each one tells you.

items.cue: flat, after your quick “Hey”, the cake bag held against her chest
options: She's delighted to see you
She'd like to talk about the wedding
She's counting, and your hello fell short
items.why: She is counting. A short hello leaves her owed, and a flat “lovely” is how owed sounds in Ruby's mouth.

traps.0: Delighted would sound like “Oh, look at you!” A flat “lovely” with a tight smile is the other thing.
traps.1: If she wanted to talk about the wedding she would have opened the cake bag. It stays shut against her chest.

items.example:
A hairdresser's, Saturday.
You say “Hi” and pick up a magazine.
“Lovely,” she says, and starts the next cut in silence.

items.cue: laughing, after five warm lines in a row
options: She's worried she is late for something
A pile of warm lines sounds like a pitch
She thinks you are teasing her about the wedding
items.why: Too many warm lines at once sound like a pitch. She is asking what you are selling.

traps.0: Worry about being late would show in her feet or her watch. She is laughing and looking at you, so the question is about the lines.
traps.2: Teasing would have a specific target, like the hat or the speeches. You gave her only a heap of warmth, and the heap is what she noticed.

items.example:
A stall at a school fair.
“Hello! Gorgeous jumper! Have a biscuit! Isn't it lovely?”
Four lines deep, you start looking for the price.

items.text: “Sorry, I've got to run, the five-a-side starts at eleven.”
items.cue: the Corner Table, after one quick hello
options: A quick exit
A compliment
A full welcome
items.why: A quick exit. It ends the greeting and counts as one small nod about your morning, not a welcome for Ruby.

traps.1: A compliment would say something nice about her. This line is about kick-off, so it can't be one.
traps.2: A full welcome needs several warm lines. One line about leaving closes the greeting instead.

items.example:
A cinema queue.
“Hi! Sorry, have to grab the tickets, back in a sec!”
A friendly exit, and still a single small nod.

rounds.label: Play, the week in motion
rounds.intro: Ruby's greeting is a counter. Pick the lines that pay what she is owed, then meet Joseph at the counter.

items.prompt: Ruby is back from her cousin's wedding after two nights away and is owed about a dozen nods. Build a greeting that pays them.

palette.text: “Wait, tell me everything about the dress.”
“I missed you. Nadia's group was dead without you.”
“Sorry, I've got to run, kick-off's at eleven.”

items.underMsg: Ruby says “Lovely.” and takes the table by the radiator on her own. She is still owed more than that.
items.overMsg: Ruby laughs. “Right. What's the catch?” A heap of warm lines sounds like a pitch.
items.hitMsg: She opens the cake bag and slides you a corner of icing.
items.why: The amount owed rises with time apart, so a weekend away asks for far more than a wave and far less than a long absence would. Too little leaves a friend flat, and too much sounds like a pitch.

items.title: Saturday, 10:20 and 10:35, the counter
items.setting: Joseph at the till of the Corner Table with a tray of teas, first when you order and then when you come back for your phone.

beats.cue: counter, 10:20, a tray of teas balanced on one hand

lines.outcome: He answers at once and sets the tray down to do it.
lines.why: A hello with his name in it is a clean exchange. It pays a nod each way.

lines.outcome: He tells the teapot it's going to rain.
lines.why: A nod with no word is smaller. It leaves him to carry the exchange alone.

beats.text: “Morning, mate. Sit anywhere except the wobbly table.”
beats.cue: still at the till, wiping a spoon

lines.outcome: He points the spoon at the window seat. “Good lad.”
lines.why: You answered what he said, not only the hello. That keeps the exchange going.

lines.outcome: You find yourself at the wobbly table. Joseph watches the saucer slide.
lines.why: The words fit, but you stopped listening halfway. It ends the exchange a half-step early.

beats.cue: counter, 10:35, second pass for the phone you left by the till. He is wiping the same patch.

lines.text: A nod and a half-smile, collect the phone.
lines.outcome: He nods back and slides the phone along the counter.
lines.why: A small nod is enough for a quick second pass. You asked for nothing, so nothing more is owed.

lines.text: “Joseph! How's the knee? Did the five-a-side move? Is your brother still abroad?”
lines.outcome: “Same as fifteen minutes ago,” he says. “What are you after?”
lines.why: Three questions on a second pass read as a favour about to be asked. The interest was real, and the pile of it felt like a pitch.

lines.text: Take the phone without looking up.
lines.outcome: Joseph, to the cloth: “Hm.”
lines.why: Going past without a look is cold, and he notices. It is a small cut that leaves him owed.

items.example:
A taxi rank.
“Evening, boss, cold one.” Every night, the same line, and the night you skip it gets noticed.

items.text: “Hey.” felt too small, and “Tell me everything about the dress” felt like too much. What explains that?
options: Time apart sets how much is owed, so too little and too much both miss
A friend who likes you will accept any greeting, so the amount never matters
Ruby is just fussy, so nothing short of a party would please her at the door
items.why: A greeting is a precise exchange. Time apart sets how much is owed. Too little leaves a gap, and too much reads as a pitch.

traps.1: If any greeting would do, Ruby's “Lovely” would not have been flat. A short hello carries a debt, and liking someone doesn't cancel it.
traps.2: “She's fussy” is a shrug, and then you stop trying. The debt stays unpaid and the flat “lovely” comes back next time.

items.example:
A friend back from a month abroad.
“Hi!” at the door, and then straight to the football.
She notices the gap in the welcome, even if nobody says so.

stories.blurb: Gwen returns to the evening class after two missed Tuesdays, and the tutor is watching the door.

opener.setting: Tuesday, 6:50pm. The corridor outside Room 14, the vending machine humming. Gwen missed the last two classes with a bad back and is walking up the corridor.

lines.text: “Gwen counts hellos. Last term someone said ‘oh, you're back’ and she sat at the far end all night.”
lines.cue: leaning on the vending machine, chewing a crisp
at the end of the corridor, folder against her chest, a plaster on her thumb

opener.ask: How much of a welcome does Gwen need after being away, and how do you build one that pays it?

rounds.label: Spot, round 1
rounds.intro: Three lines from the hello in the corridor. Tap what each one tells you.

items.cue: after your quick “Hi”, sitting down with her folder at the end of the row
options: She's counting, and your hello was short
She's keen to get on with the group task
She's still cross about her last feedback sheet
items.why: She is counting. A short hello leaves her owed, and a flat “right” is how owed sounds from the end of a row.

traps.1: Keen would come with a pen already out and a question about the task. Her folder stays shut, so the “right” is closing the talk.
traps.2: Cross about the sheet would come with a sheet in her hand and a name attached. Nothing here points at feedback, only at your hello.

items.example:
A supermarket checkout.
You say “Hi” and keep scrolling.
“Right,” says the cashier, and scans the next item without a word.

items.text: “Okay, which one of you wants my notes?”
items.cue: laughing, after a run of warm lines at the classroom door
options: She's bored of the welcome and wants the class to begin
She's tired from the pain and wants to be left alone
She thinks you're angling for her notes
items.why: Too many warm lines at once sound like a pitch. She is guessing what the pile is for.

traps.0: Boredom would mean the welcome dragged. It was warm, not dull, so the question is about the warmth.
traps.1: Tired and sore would sound like “Not now.” She is joking and looking at you, so she is checking the motive.

items.example:
A lecture hall.
“Hello! Love your bag! Did you get lunch? Are you free later?”
“What do you need?” she says. Too much warmth looks like a pitch.

items.text: “Sorry, I need to photocopy the reading list before Mr Ashby starts.”
items.cue: the corridor, after a quick hello
options: A compliment
A quick exit
A full welcome
items.why: A quick exit. It ends the greeting and counts as one small nod about your evening, not a welcome for Gwen.

traps.0: A compliment would say something nice about her. This line is about photocopying, so it can't be one.
traps.2: A full welcome needs several warm lines. One line about the reading list closes the greeting instead.

items.example:
A staff kitchen.
“Morning! Sorry, I've got a meeting, catch you later!”
Friendly, and still a single small nod.

rounds.label: Play, the week in motion
rounds.intro: Gwen's greeting is a counter. Pick the lines that pay what she is owed, then meet Mr Ashby at the door.

items.prompt: Gwen is back after missing the last two Tuesdays and is owed about a dozen nods. Build a greeting that pays them.

palette.text: “Wait, tell me everything the physio said.”
“I missed you. Room 14 was far too quiet without you.”
“Sorry, I need to photocopy the reading list.”

items.underMsg: Gwen says “Right.” and opens her folder to a page that doesn't need reading. She is still owed more than that.
items.overMsg: Gwen laughs. “Okay, which one of you wants my notes?” A pile of warm lines sounds like a pitch.
items.hitMsg: She puts the folder down and tells you what the physio did with a cushion.
items.why: The amount owed rises with time apart, so two missed weeks asks for far more than a wave across the room and far less than a term away would. Too little leaves a classmate flat, and too much sounds like a pitch.

items.title: Tuesday, 6:55 and 7:10pm, Room 14
items.setting: Mr Ashby at the door of Room 14 with the sign-in clipboard, first as you arrive and then when you go back for the pen you dropped.

beats.cue: the door of Room 14, 6:55, the sign-in clipboard held against his chest

lines.outcome: He looks up from the list and ticks you off with a flourish.
lines.why: A hello with his name in it is a clean exchange. It pays a nod each way.

lines.outcome: He ticks you off without looking and tells the list it's a cold one.
lines.why: A nod with no word is smaller. It leaves him to carry the exchange alone.

beats.text: “Evening. Your draft's on the front desk. Read the margin comments before you argue with them.”
beats.cue: still at the door, pen behind his ear

lines.outcome: He taps the clipboard twice. “Good. They're mostly fair.”
lines.why: You answered what he said, not only the hello. That keeps the exchange going.

lines.outcome: “Yes, yes,” he says to your back, and goes on holding the door.
lines.why: The words fit, but you were already inside. It ends the exchange a half-step early.

beats.cue: the corridor, 7:10, second pass for the pen you dropped. He is ticking the last names.

lines.text: A nod and a half-smile, then keep moving.
lines.outcome: He nods back and finishes the tick.
lines.why: A small nod is enough for a quick second pass. You asked for nothing, so nothing more is owed.

lines.text: “Mr Ashby! How was your weekend? Did the exam board reply? Is the heating getting fixed?”
lines.outcome: “I saw you at 6:55,” he says. “What do you want?”
lines.why: Three questions on a second pass read as a favour about to be asked. The interest was real, and the pile of it felt like a pitch.

lines.outcome: Mr Ashby, to the clipboard: “Hm.”
lines.why: Going by without a look is cold, and he notices. It is a small cut that leaves him owed.

items.example:
A porter in a hospital lobby.
“Morning, doctor, mind the wet floor.” Same line every shift, and a shift without it gets noticed.

items.text: “Hi, Gwen.” felt too small, and “Tell me everything the physio said” felt like too much. What explains that?
options: Gwen is touchy about her absence, so nothing you say will count for much
Classmates only owe each other politeness, so any line is fine whatever the gap
Time apart sets how much is owed, so too little and too much both land wrong
items.why: A greeting is a precise exchange. Time apart sets how much is owed. Too little leaves a gap, and too much reads as a pitch.

traps.0: Touchy sounds like a shrug, and then you stop trying. The debt stays unpaid, so the flat “right” comes back next week.
traps.1: If politeness were all that was owed, any amount would do. Gwen's “Right.” came after a short hello because a short hello carries a debt.

items.example:
A teammate back after a fortnight's leave.
“Hi!” at the desk, and then straight to the spreadsheet.
She notices the gap in the welcome, even if nobody says so.
